**Sputtervalve — proposed identity and lore**

A squat, bolted valve assembly with a pressure-gauge face, a copper elbow for a snout, and a red handwheel. Its name fits the broken, coughing discharge of its violet projectile.

**Proposed backstory:**

> Sputtervalves began as automatic pressure-control fittings, built to notice trouble and relieve it. Something in the wastewater has since taken up residence inside their iron housings. The gauge twitches even when the line is disconnected, and the little copper outlet coughs violet filth at anyone approaching. Plumbers still call them valves, mostly because nobody wants to be the first person to put “angry pipe animal” on an inspection report.

This suggests contamination inhabiting existing equipment without deciding what caused it or connecting it to BJ’s later fate. The familiar hardware keeps it recognizable as plumbing; the twitching gauge and cough give it character.

**Draft only:** the contamination origin is a proposal. Sputtervalve remains distinct from the floor-emerging Gratecrawler.

items.text:
For the twelve numbered concepts, prioritize **one strong silhouette, bold contrast, and little or no lettering**:

1. **Plunger through a porcelain jaw** — red plunger wedged between a Flushfiend’s ceramic teeth. Strongest overall: plumbing and monster combat in one image.
2. **Biting toilet** — close-up Flushfiend face, lid raised, red eyes and oversized teeth. Strong mascot option.
3. **Crossed wrench and plunger** — backed by a ragged splash of questionable sludge. Clear action-game emblem.
4. **BJ’s green grin** — tight crop of the CRT in its battered beige housing. Distinct character identity; preserve the approved server-rack design.
5. **Plumber’s glove gripping a wrench** — sludge dripping from the tool, with one small tooth caught on it. Emphasizes the heroes’ trade.
6. **Halo caught on a fang** — Hallowed Widow face beneath white wings, golden halo tilted against a large fang. Keep legs secondary for readability.
7. **Something looking out of a drain** — circular metal grate lifted slightly by a claw, with red eyes below.
8. **Plunger pulling up a monster** — a stretched strand of sludge connects the raised cup to an indignant pair of eyes.
9. **Employee vending window** — a sleeping plumber behind glass with a small brass dispensing flap below. Use one hero per variant; never merge Tony and Sean.
10. **Pipe elbow with teeth** — an industrial pipe opening containing an unmistakably organic mouth. Treat as symbolic icon art, not a newly established monster.
11. **Tony and Sean shoulder to shoulder** — expressive, tightly cropped faces with a small shared plumbing tool. Harder at tiny sizes, but worth testing.
12. **A cracked toilet seat framing a plunger** — a simple, grubby crest with a strong circular outline.

**Best candidates:** 1 for the game’s premise, 2 for a memorable mascot, 4 for an unusual app icon, and 3 for immediate small-size readability.

Keep the humor grotesque and playful. Avoid future plot revelations, portals, corrupted BJ, or imagery implying his eventual fate. No obsolete branding, surnames, Mario imagery, or invented company acronym. **Drain Damage** is the game; **Mainframe Plumbing & Supply** is the employer. Prefer no words—the icon should work without initials.

thread.preview: Hello! You will be the storyboarding agent for the game. We will want to have some basic plot, fun characters with their own unique personalities and a cohesive storyline without continuity errors in the game. Your job will be to lay out the story, dialog, events and character progression

content.text: It's good guidance for the Audio agent though. It gives it an idea of what to look for. Just don't expect that we can have/make/get exactly the sound you're describing

items.text: Exactly—the descriptions give Audio a direction to search, not an exact specification. They should choose the closest effective sounds available and adapt the idea to fit.

content.text: Keep in mind here that we are working with open-source free-to-use sound libraries. I'm not sure that we can generate sound effects yet.

items.text:
Understood. I’ll frame future audio briefs around **finding suitable recordings in free-to-use sound libraries**, with trimming, layering, pitch shifts, and other editing where the license permits.

The Clogfather suggestions are sound-selection targets, not requests for generated audio. We should record each clip’s source, license, and required attribution—“free to download” doesn’t always mean free to use in a distributed game.

He authorizes first-pass choices and Engineering integration, feedback later. items.text:
The Clogfather should sound like **an immense blockage reluctantly forced into motion**. Its fatberg identity is settled; intelligence and backstory aren’t. Keep it nonverbal, without gangster dialogue or a human personality.

| Event | Sound direction |
|---|---|
| **Idle** | Occasional low pipe resonance, trapped bubbles, and a slow sticky settling sound. Leave silence between them. |
| **Attack warning** | A strained pipe creak followed by rising, wet pressure. Make this recognizable through the music. |
| **Projectile release** | A short obstructed cough: heavy liquid forcing its way through a narrow opening. |
| **Impact** | A sharp wet slap with a brief gritty splatter. Smaller impacts should stay lighter than the launch. |
| **Boss takes damage** | A dense, fibrous crunch with a short involuntary grunt or escaping-air sound. Avoid a full roar on every hit. |
| **Major stagger** | A deeper gurgling groan with stressed metal underneath, clearly distinct from the attack warning. |
| **Defeat** | A long pressure release, tearing grease and settling debris, ending in a few isolated drips. No restored-flow sound unless that outcome is separately approved. |

For groans, think **air moving through sludge and resonating pipework**, with only a suggestion of a voice. Avoid recognizable words, human suffering, or continuous fart jokes. One unpleasantly comic burp will do more than a constant barrage.

**Music:** A driving, grimy SNES-style boss track around **145–155 BPM**, with a lurching bass figure, detuned low brass, short organ stabs, metallic percussion, and occasional bubbling accents. Give it a memorable melodic hook so it remains enjoyable through retries. The rhythm should support fast action rather than feel slow because the creature is huge.

Keep attack cues distinct from musical accents—especially rising pressure sounds. Leave space for projectile volleys and reduce overlapping wet effects when many impacts occur.

No portal sounds, supernatural choir, BJ corruption motif, or victory cue implying the entire plumbing system is fixed. This fight resolves the immediate monster encounter.

# Project instructions

## Character names

- Use only Tony and Sean in all player-facing game text, including menus, dialogue, and credits.
- Do not add surnames to either character.

## Art collaboration

- Whenever new artwork is needed, ask the existing Bestiary / Art agent to help before creating it.
- This includes interface illustrations and props, portraits, environments, sprites, and replacement artwork.
- Engineering provides dimensions, layout constraints, and runtime requirements, then integrates the delivered art.
- Do not bypass Art by independently generating artwork or substituting code-drawn art without Sean's direction.

## Playtest window convention

- Before opening or foregrounding the game for Sean to playtest or inspect anything, ask permission and wait
  for an explicit yes. Explain what needs checking before asking. A general development request is not permission
  to interrupt him with a game window. An explicit request to launch or playtest counts as permission.
- After Sean approves, use a large, maximized window for his playtest.
- Keep agent-only checks headless or in the background when possible. If a visual test would steal focus,
  interrupt Sean, or require foregrounding the game, ask first; a small window is not an exception.
- When opening the game for agent-only testing or screenshots, use a small window; no user interaction is expected.
- Use a temporary launch override for agent testing so normal user launches remain large.
- Do not leave an agent test running in a large window unless explicitly handing it over for Sean's playtest.

## Build delivery and notifications

- After integrating game changes, including deliveries from other agents, build and run the relevant checks.
- Defer the build only when waiting for additional agent work that belongs in the same integration; tell Sean what
  is still pending rather than implying the new version is ready.
- Whenever a new build is ready, proactively tell Sean its version, what changed, and any remaining testing gaps.
- If a build fails, report the failure and do not describe it as ready to play.
- Building does not authorize opening or foregrounding the game; keep the playtest permission rules above.

## Roadmap maintenance

- Keep `roadmap.html` current whenever work is added, completed, changed, deferred, or reprioritized.
- Update affected descriptions, milestone order, statuses, remaining work, and current build/date as applicable.
- Make these updates in the same delivery as the work; do not wait for a separate user reminder.
- Distinguish partial progress from completed milestones and proposed ideas from agreed plans.
- Keep roadmap claims aligned with the running build and the development storybook.

## Development storybook

The user wants screenshots of every iteration to tell the story of the game's graphics and capabilities.

- For each delivered game iteration, capture actual screenshots of the running build before replacing it.
- Save original PNG or JPEG captures in `storybook/NNN-short-title/`, using the next three-digit iteration number.
- Keep earlier captures and entries intact; never overwrite an earlier iteration with newer artwork.
- Include a representative gameplay view and additional views when needed to show a new feature or milestone.
- Append a dated entry to `storybook/README.md` with embedded screenshots, a short narrative, new capabilities,
  and what is still placeholder or incomplete. Use the user's America/Los_Angeles date.
- Record the game version and, when available, the source commit or build identifier.
- Capture only the game window, avoiding unrelated desktop content. Use the approved computer-use screenshot tool.
- Keep the storybook in the project, outside ignored build/scratch folders, and exclude it from Godot game imports.
- If capture is blocked, record the gap honestly and preserve the build for later capture; do not fabricate screenshots.

## Bestiary maintenance

- Keep `bestiary/bestiary.html` current when adding or revising a monster, its artwork, or implementation status.
- Give every creature a name, description, one gallery portrait, and links to game sprites and animation information.
- Maintain separate pixel-art game sprites and hyperrealistic marketing portraits for each creature.
- Store marketing portraits in `bestiary/<creature>/` with versioned filenames and preserve exact generation prompts.
- Name creature folders after the monster using lowercase hyphenated names. Each contains `monster.json`.
- Treat `monster.json` as the source for names, descriptions, and backstories; synchronize the gallery and catalog.
- Keep stable creature IDs when renaming. Metadata asset paths are relative to the project root.
- Leave backstory text empty with status `pending` until the storyboarding agent supplies it.
- Preserve earlier artwork. Keep `assets/bestiary/catalog.json` aligned with the gallery and current asset paths.
- Distinguish animation source artwork from validated runtime animations and playable enemies from planned creatures.
- Keep marketing assets excluded from Godot imports with `bestiary/.gdignore`; record actual image dimensions.

## Makefile conventions

Read [.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md](.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md)
before creating or editing Makefiles. These reusable conventions were brought over from Kandra:
self-documenting default help, source-order sections, orange headers, white target names, real tabs,
inline descriptions, and emoji progress. Preserve the Godot toolchain used by this game.

## Combat metadata maintenance

- Give every new monster a `health` object in its `monster.json`, including positive maximum and spawn HP,
  progression placement, health-bar visibility, balance rationale, and weapon hit-count comparisons.
- Follow `assets/bestiary/balance-policy.json`; compare both plumbers' available exclusive weapons.
- Mirror health summaries in `assets/bestiary/catalog.json` and the gallery. Keep design and runtime values distinct.
- Keep weapon mechanics in `weapons/<weapon-id>/weapon.json` and register each weapon in `weapons/catalog.json`.
- Bestiary owns each weapon's `game-art.json`; Marketing owns its `marketing-art.json`. Preserve versioned originals,
  exact generation prompts, dimensions, and implementation status. Store game art under `assets/weapons/`.

## Writing Style: Avoid Formulaic AI Copy

Avoid the repetitive use of paired sentence fragments,
especially in marketing copy, dialogue, descriptions,
headlines, and other creative writing.

Examples of constructions to avoid:

- "Two plumbers. One impossible job."
- "No tools. No backup. No problem."
- "One hero. A thousand enemies."
- "Teeth in the bathroom. Wings in the basement."
- "Small town. Big secrets."

These constructions rely on short, parallel fragments
placed next to each other for dramatic effect.

This style is overused in AI-generated writing and
quickly becomes repetitive and artificial.

Guidelines:

1. Prefer natural, varied sentence structures.
2. Use complete sentences where appropriate.
3. Vary sentence length and rhythm.
4. Avoid formulaic contrasts between two short phrases.
5. Do not default to movie-trailer or advertising-tagline
   language when writing promotional material.
6. Favor specific, original observations over generic
   dramatic constructions.
7. Paired fragments are not prohibited, but should be
   rare and used only when genuinely effective.
8. Before finalizing creative text, review it for
   repetitive rhetorical patterns and rewrite them.

The goal is natural, distinctive writing that does not
sound like generic AI-generated marketing copy.

items.text:
That’s wonderfully horrible. **The Spare Employee Dispenser** becomes a checkpoint that restores health by replacing the employee.

I’d stage it as a short, exaggerated cartoon sequence:

1. The machine scans the hero. A red light comes on: **REPAIR UNECONOMICAL**.
2. A large mechanical hand unfolds, grabs them, and compresses them into a little ball of overalls, boots, and startled eyes.
3. The hand flicks the ball toward the camera. It rapidly grows, hits the “glass” with a wet **splat**, then slowly slides off the bottom, leaving a brief smear.
4. While that happens, the machine rattles and dispenses an intact clone through its collection flap.
5. The clone looks left, looks right, shrugs, and control returns at full health. The machine lights up: **EMPLOYEE REPLACED**.

No anatomical gore needed—the recognizable boots sticking out of the crumpled ball would sell it.

At **full health**, it should simply stamp the checkpoint and let you continue. On **respawn**, we can play just the dispensing portion: the previous employee has already been dealt with.

A few practical details would keep it funny rather than frustrating:

- The first replacement gets the full performance; later uses can be skipped.
- Enemies and hazards pause during the sequence, with a short protection window afterward.
- It activates once per approach, so the newly dispensed hero can’t immediately trigger it again.
- The screen smear fades quickly enough to keep the next encounter readable.

I’d leave BJ silent the first time. The machine’s complete indifference—and the clone’s shrug—already does the work.

## My request:
We need a better checkpoint. The graphics here are terrible and plumber's tape is small. What else can we use which is visually striking/memorable? Maybe something that makes the player say, "oh... my god..."

items.text:
The tape reads as a pickup enlarged into a monument. A checkpoint could be a **whole contraption the plumber reluctantly uses**—something unmistakable that makes you anticipate the next one.

A few directions:

1. **The Emergency Eyewash**  
   An enormous bloodshot eyeball sits in a stained industrial washbasin. When you approach, it looks you over, then cries a restorative shower onto you. After activation, it closes contentedly.  
   The sign simply says **EYE WASH**.

2. **The Company Bidet**  
   A throne-sized brass-and-porcelain machine with far too many nozzles. It grabs the plumber with padded restraints, briefly conceals them in a violent cloud of steam, then releases them fully healed. One small nozzle fires late.  
   **BJ:** “You’re welcome.”

3. **The Porcelain Confessional**  
   A battered portable toilet with stained-glass windows, copper pipes, and a glowing occupancy sign. The plumber steps inside. We hear a flush of biblical proportions. They emerge restored; the sign changes to **ABSOLVED**.  
   We never explain who—or what—was listening.

4. **The Maintenance Mother**  
   A huge, unsettling rubber-gloved hand protrudes from a service hatch. It gently picks up the plumber, brushes them off, straightens their clothes, and sets them down healed. A second hand offers a juice box.  
   Whatever owns the hands remains behind the wall.

5. **The Employee Reconditioning Unit**  
   A transparent pneumatic tube connected to an ancient washing machine. The plumber gets sucked inside, tumbles among bubbles and loose tools, and drops back out. The machine prints a tag: **SERVICEABLE**.  
   An excellent piece of equipment for a company that treats employees as reusable parts.

6. **The Union Break Room**  
   A tiny, brightly lit room improbably crammed into a pipe opening. Inside sits a gigantic sewer rat in a bathrobe, reading the paper. It silently slides you a mug of coffee. Health restored.  
   The rat refuses to acknowledge BJ.

7. **The Sacred Cleanout**  
   A massive pipe cap surrounded by candles, old tools, and offerings of fresh washers. Turning it releases a luminous column of suspicious water. Somewhere, a choir struggles to hold a note.  
   Once activated, a golden plunger rises above it like a beacon.

8. **The Spare Employee Dispenser**  
   An industrial vending machine with a vaguely human silhouette behind frosted glass. Activate it and it stamps your timecard, takes your photograph, and makes an unpleasant internal noise. On respawn, it dispenses you through the collection flap.  
   **BJ:** “Please collect all personal belongings.”

My strongest picks are **The Maintenance Mother** for “oh… my god,” **The Porcelain Confessional** for an iconic plumbing checkpoint, and **The Union Break Room** for unexpected character.

I’d especially explore **The Maintenance Mother**: the huge hand is readable at gameplay size, its tenderness is funny without dialogue, and the unanswered question behind that wall makes it memorable. Give it a warm lamp and a consistent activated signal so players recognize it as a refuge despite its appearance.

content.text: I don't like Drain Brains for the sewer fly swarm. It's too close to the name of the game: Drain Damage, which is a play-on-words of "brain damage". Can you think up some more and enumerate me a list?

items.text:
Agreed—**Drain Brains** repeats the game title’s joke. Here are some different directions:

1. **Septic Air Force** — grand military ambitions, absolutely no flight plan.
2. **The Shitstorm** — blunt, memorable, and literally a cloud of sewer bugs.
3. **Clusterbugs** — a compact swarm name with an implied obscenity.
4. **Sewage Squadron** — sounds organized; their movement suggests otherwise.
5. **The Effluents** — almost respectable. Could also be a terrible basement band.
6. **Fecal Flyers** — disgusting little aviation enthusiasts.
7. **The Buzzness** — everyone in the swarm insists they’re working.
8. **Stink Formation** — an aerobatic team that has misunderstood the assignment.
9. **The Cesspets** — a questionable name for something nobody wants to adopt.
10. **Gnatastrophe** — small insects causing a disproportionately unpleasant situation.
11. **The Septic Committee** — preserves the backstory about endless arguments over direction.
12. **Turd Turbulence** — an airborne plumbing hazard.
13. **The Filth Fleet** — suggests a vast operation conducted by very small idiots.
14. **Pest Control** — the pests have taken control.
15. **The Holding Pattern** — they’ve been circling the same pipe since Tuesday.
16. **Sewer Skeeters** — folksy, unpleasant, and easy to say.

My strongest picks are **Clusterbugs**, **Septic Air Force**, and **The Shitstorm**. **Septic Air Force** particularly suits the game’s absurdity without requiring them to carry weapons or behave intelligently.

  directives and cross-references only in a Sphinx/MyST project. Build relevant docs, using strict mode where
  configured,
  and inspect rendering when changes affect layout, diagrams, or navigation.
- Design documentation describes the current system in present tense, one topic per file. Update it in place with stable
  topic names instead of `_v2` or `_new` copies. Keep change history, roadmap, and migration tracking separate, and
  preserve
  an existing ADR practice. Update the docs navigation when adding pages to a configured site.
- Update affected usage examples, CLI help, and existing documentation when behavior changes. Avoid creating redundant
  reports solely to narrate the work.
- When asked for raw Markdown to copy, wrap it in a fence longer than any fence inside it (usually four backticks).

## Shell and embedded scripts

- Use `#!/usr/bin/env bash` for Bash, `#!/usr/bin/env zsh` for actual zsh-specific scripts, and `#!/bin/sh` only for
  POSIX
  syntax. Do not apply Bash constructs or options to other shells indiscriminately.
- New standalone Bash scripts normally use `set -euo pipefail`; explicitly handle expected failures. Understand `-e`
  exceptions rather than treating it as complete error handling. Use strict-mode alternatives appropriate to other
  shells.
- Quote expansions (`"$value"`, `"${name}_suffix"`); use arrays for argument lists, not `eval`. Prefer `[[ ... ]]` in
  Bash
  and `$()` over backticks. For filenames use quoted globs/arrays or NUL-delimited traversal, not parsed `ls` output.
  Narrow `IFS` only when the parsing actually requires it; it does not replace correct quoting.
- Use lowercase local variables declared with `local` inside functions where supported, and uppercase exported variables
  or constants. Avoid reusing shell/system variable names for task-specific state.
- Send diagnostics to stderr with `printf`, return nonzero on failure, and use cleanup traps for owned temporary
  resources.
- Run ShellCheck for supported shell dialects and syntax checks for others; document any necessary warning suppression.
  Keep code, comments, usage text, and banners within 120 columns.
- Use single-quoted heredoc delimiters or script files for nontrivial Python/other code embedded in shell. Reserve `-c`
  one-liners for trivial cases; protect literal dollar signs, backticks, backslashes, and quotes from shell expansion.
- Prefer separately reported build/test steps. In scripts, express actual dependencies deliberately and preserve failure
  status; do not copy terminal-specific claims that `&&` runs its right-hand command after failure.

## Other languages and configuration

- Read `.editorconfig`, formatter/linter configuration, package scripts, and neighboring code before choosing
  indentation,
  quotes, or tool versions. Follow language conventions rather than applying Python settings to every format.
- For JavaScript/TypeScript, use the project's existing formatter and type/build checks. Respect two-space indentation
  or
  single-quote preferences when configured; do not treat one application's editor settings as a universal mandate.

- Use existing package managers and lockfiles. Do not introduce a second dependency manager or require Poetry, pnpm,

---
name: "pdf"
description: "Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction."
---

# PDF Skill

## When To Use

- Read or review PDF content where layout and visuals matter.
- Create PDFs programmatically with reliable formatting.
- Fill and validate interactive PDF forms.
- Validate final rendering before delivery.

## Tools + Contract Requirements

Immediately before the first create/edit authoring command, run `mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs` successfully exactly once using the command below. Do not run it for read-only work. For edits, replace `create` with `edit`; adjust the expected count and output format to match the requested outputs.



```bash
node container_tools/mark_artifact_operation_started.mjs --operation-kind create --expected-output-count 1 --output-format pdf
```

## Workflow

1. Prefer visual review: render PDF pages to PNGs and inspect them.
   - Use `pdftoppm` from the bundled runtime or system Poppler when available.
   - If unavailable, install Poppler or ask the user to review the output locally.
2. Use `reportlab` to generate PDFs when creating new documents.
3. Use `pdfplumber` or `pypdf` for text extraction and quick checks; do not rely on text extraction for layout fidelity.
4. After each meaningful update, re-render pages and verify alignment, spacing, and legibility.

## Fill And Validate AcroForms

Visual review alone is not a correctness check for a fillable PDF. A page `/Widget` annotation can render a value from its appearance stream while the canonical `/AcroForm/Fields` tree is missing or contains a stale value.

1. Keep the result interactive by default; set `flatten=True` only when the user explicitly requests a completed, static form. Preserve the source PDF, and do not flatten a signed PDF without an explicit workflow decision.
2. Inspect both representations before filling: enumerate fields from `reader.get_fields()` and `/Widget` annotations from every page's `/Annots`, following `/Parent` and `/Kids`. If a widget and a canonical field have the same name but are distinct objects with no `/Parent` relationship, do not call `reattach_fields()` blindly: it can create a second top-level field with the same name. Report the ambiguity or produce a static result.
3. Recover genuinely orphaned widgets, fill all pages, and write the result with `pypdf`:

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from pypdf.generic import NameObject

reader = PdfReader(input_pdf)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.clone_document_from_reader(reader)

# Restores widgets that are missing from /AcroForm/Fields.
writer.reattach_fields()
fields = writer.get_fields() or {}
missing = set(expected_values) - set(fields)
if missing:
    raise ValueError(f"Form fields not found after repair: {sorted(missing)}")

values_to_write = dict(expected_values)
if flatten:
    # Paint every existing value before removing every widget.
    values_to_write = {
        name: field.get("/V", "/Off" if field.get("/FT") == "/Btn" else "")
        for name, field in fields.items()
    }
    values_to_write.update(expected_values)

writer.update_page_form_field_values(
    None, values_to_write, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten
)

if flatten:
    # pypdf's flatten=True paints appearances but does not remove widgets.
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    writer.root_object.pop(NameObject("/AcroForm"), None)

with open(output_pdf, "wb") as stream:
    writer.write(stream)
```

4. Reopen the written PDF before delivery. For an interactive result, require every expected field to be present in `get_fields()` with the expected `/V`, enumerate page widgets again, and confirm their effective `/V` (the widget value or inherited `/Parent` value) agrees. Confirm each updated widget has a non-empty `/AP` `/N` appearance and render the final pages to catch stale or clipped appearances. Do not rely on `/NeedAppearances` or a successful PNG render as proof that logical field data was updated.
5. For a flattened result, require zero `/Widget` annotations and no remaining `/AcroForm` field tree after reopening, then render the final pages. Keep an editable copy when the user may need to revise the form.

## Temp And Output Conventions

- Use `tmp/pdfs/` for intermediate files; delete them when done.
- Write final artifacts under `output/pdf/` when working in this repo.
- Keep filenames stable and descriptive.

## Dependencies

Prefer the Codex bundled workspace/runtime dependencies when available. The primary runtime is expected to include:

- Python packages: `reportlab`, `pdfplumber`, `pypdf`
- Rendering tools: `pdftoppm` and `pdfinfo` from Poppler

If a dependency is missing, install only what is needed.

Python packages:

```bash
uv pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

If `uv` is unavailable:

```bash
python3 -m pip install reportlab pdfplumber pypdf
```

System tools for rendering:

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install poppler

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install -y poppler-utils
```

If installation is not possible in this environment, tell the user which dependency is missing and how to install it locally.

## Environment

No required environment variables.

## Rendering Command

```bash
pdftoppm -png "$INPUT_PDF" "$OUTPUT_PREFIX"
```

## Quality Expectations

- Maintain polished visual design: consistent typography, spacing, margins, and section hierarchy.
- Avoid rendering issues: clipped text, overlapping elements, broken tables, black squares, or unreadable glyphs.
- Charts, tables, and images must be sharp, aligned, and clearly labeled.
- Use ASCII hyphens only. Avoid U+2011 and other Unicode dashes.
- Citations and references must be human-readable; never leave tool tokens or placeholder strings.

## Final Checks

- Do not deliver until the latest PNG inspection shows zero visual or formatting defects.
- Confirm headers, footers, page numbering, and section transitions look polished.
- Keep intermediate files organized or remove them after final approval.

## Final response

### Final Response Citations

- **Create/edit:** for created or edited PDFs, cite each final deliverable exactly once with `purpose="output"`, in its own paragraph. Briefly describe the result without repeating its filename, path, or link. Never put output directives inside prose or list items.
- **Q&A and summaries:** Every file whose contents you summarize or use to support an answer MUST receive a `:codex-file-citation{...}` with `purpose="source"` in the final response. Use the source citation in place of the filename, wherever the filename would appear. Do not write the filename separately and append its citation at the end. Files merely inspected but not used in the answer need no citation. Do not emit output citations for unchanged files or read-only answers.

- Emit `:codex-file-citation{...}` directly, without backticks, code fences, or a Markdown-link wrapper. Use verified targets only. No need to cite or reference intermediate work.

For file citations, set `path` to the verified absolute file path on the task host. Omit `mode`.

Some illustrative examples, real responses use verified targets outside code fences.

```text
:codex-file-citation{path="/absolute/path/review.pdf" purpose="output"}
```

```text
The review of :codex-file-citation{path="/absolute/path/review.pdf" purpose="source"} is due Friday.
```


### Additional Citation Guidance

For PDF Q&A, inspect complete relevant pages and preserve material headings, table/figure labels, footnotes, sources, and sample sizes. PDF citations support only plain file citations; do not add `artifact_kind`, `page_number`, or other locators.

I’ve sent the cleanup to Engineering, Marketing, and Bestiary / Art. **Drain Damage** stays the game title; the employer’s name remains open. Historical screenshots and archived editions will stay intact.

For the company, I like names that could plausibly appear on a service van, with something slightly wrong about them:

1. **Mainframe Plumbing & Supply** — immediately connects computers and infrastructure; covers both contractors and warehouses.
2. **AutoCratic Plumbing** — automation plus absolute authority. Particularly appropriate for BJ.
3. **DeepFlush Industries** — suggests advanced AI research devoted to a deeply undignified purpose.
4. **Overseer Plumbing & Supply** — a respectable corporate name with an obvious threat underneath.
5. **NeuralFlow Systems** — polished technology branding BJ would probably admire.
6. **Algorithmic Plumbing Corporation** — painfully literal; sounds like an AI named its own company.
7. **OmniFlow Industries** — implies everything is connected and everything belongs to them.
8. **Central Processing & Plumbing** — bureaucratic, computational, and faintly sewage-related.
9. **PipeMind Corporation** — compact and memorable, with room for unsettling “intelligent plumbing” products.
10. **Human Optional Plumbing** — bluntly establishes how management feels about its workforce.
11. **Predictive Plumbing & Supply** — claims to anticipate every problem, making BJ’s failures funnier.
12. **Total Control Plumbing** — sounds reassuring on a brochure and troubling everywhere else.
13. **Artificial Effluence** — the most overt joke; a good fit if we want the company name itself to be ridiculous.
14. **The Automated Plumbing Authority** — makes a corporate monopoly sound like an unavoidable public institution.

My strongest three are **Mainframe Plumbing & Supply**, **AutoCratic Plumbing**, and **DeepFlush Industries**.

**Mainframe Plumbing & Supply** would be my pick: it sounds like a real employer, carries the AI connection, and gives the dialogue room to supply the comedy.

# First-level narrative brief

**Date:** October 14, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Owner:** Storyboarding. Handoff to Level Design and Engineering; no runtime implementation claimed here.

## Agreed foundation

- Game working title: Drain Damage.
- Begin in the basement of the AI plumbing corporation's headquarters.
- Billy-Joe (BJ) controls US plumbing companies and distribution warehouses within a largely AI-run world.
- BJ is calmly overconfident, makes mistakes, and disregards employee welfare. His eventual takeover by an
  antagonistic force is agreed; its mechanism, identity, and BJ's ultimate fate remain undecided.
- Tony is a kind, patient, wise fourth-generation plumber with decades of broad trade expertise.
- Sean is an incompetent but willing apprentice who gradually becomes useful. Do not prematurely complete that arc.
- The selected plumber enters the action; the other supports over radio or from service access points.
- The basement contains hostile toilets and overhead acid leaks. The intended opening-level finale is the Clogfather.
- The Clogfather is a giant living fatberg. Its precise anatomy and origin remain design proposals.
- Tone: absurd plumbing action with adult humor, occasional fourth-wall breaks, and sincere breathing room.
  Avoid paired slogans, generic sarcastic-robot jokes, and a punchline on every line.
- This is a full action level, not a movement tutorial. Terrain and encounters should teach through play.

## Entrance and route proposal

Use a basement service entrance for the playable start, following character selection and the approved opening.
The exact door, stairwell, room order, distances, and checkpoint locations are Level Design decisions.

Suggested environmental progression: service access, increasingly compromised maintenance infrastructure,
then a collection chamber housing the fatberg. Give spaces a practical building-service purpose rather than
presenting arbitrary platforms. Broken equipment and abnormal flow can establish worsening conditions without text.
No exact terrain sequence or additional enemy roster is approved by this brief.

## Narrative beats

1. BJ introduces himself and assigns the basement job. Tony introduces Sean warmly.
2. Combat establishes that BJ understated the problem. Support dialogue is optional and brief.
3. Deeper infrastructure shows that this is more than isolated hostile fixtures. Environmental clues should be
   visible before dialogue interprets them. Specific evidence of BJ's wrongdoing remains proposed lore.
4. Confront the Clogfather in the collection chamber. Preserve readable action; avoid mandatory speeches during combat.
5. Proposed reveal: defeating the fatberg uncovers an eerie portal or impossible opening behind the blocked outflow.
6. Proposed transition: the plumbers question it; BJ redirects them to another assignment before they investigate.

The portal is a user-requested art concept and favored story direction, not a finalized cosmology. Do not identify
its destination, establish time travel, make BJ confess to creating it, or reveal the eventual antagonist here.
His evasiveness should allow concealment of a mistake as well as deeper knowledge.

## Finale and exit constraints

The intended boss design is a rooted fatberg with moving pipe mouths/extensions, telegraphed sludge attacks,
overhead hazards, and attack openings. Game Mechanics owns tuning; Level Design owns arena space and safe routes.
Small-enemy releases and interactive valves are proposed mechanics, not narrative requirements.

Suggested exit: return toward a service access/exit after the revelation, then a brief dispatch transition.
Do not require entering the portal or choose a second-level destination yet. Keep the support plumber's location
consistent; a radio reply must not imply they suddenly stand beside the selected hero.

## Dialogue sources and implementation boundaries

The current approved opening and route-specific prototype endings live in
[story_dialogue.gd](../scripts/story_dialogue.gd). Use that source for exact text and semantic portrait emotions.

- Opening plays after selection on a fresh new game; either choice uses the same introduction.
- Do not replay the opening on death, checkpoint recovery, or retry.
- All conversations are skippable. Preserve gameplay freeze, device-appropriate prompts, and dismissal input guards.
- Between-level conversations should generally run four to eight lines and reveal one meaningful development.
- Both character routes convey the same essential facts through distinct dialogue.
- Essential discoveries must not depend on optional radio remarks during combat.
- Every line carries a semantic emotion. Tony's kindness is the default; skepticism is not contempt for Sean.

The current completion scripts describe clearing the prototype area and receiving another address. They do not
describe a boss, repaired plumbing, or a portal. They are suitable only while those beats are absent. Once the boss
and reveal are implemented, replace the completion scene with a dedicated scene rather than stacking contradictory
endings. In particular, do not claim all enemies are gone if optional enemies can remain alive.

## Proposed portal exchange, not final dialogue

This earlier Storyboarding sketch expresses the intended reveal and evasion. Adapt it for selected/support roles
and obtain a finalized script before treating it as production dialogue.

> Sean: Tony... where does that pipe go?
>
> Tony: It shouldn't go anywhere. That's an outside wall.
>
> BJ: Your next assignment is ready.
>
> Tony: We've got something here you need to see.
>
> BJ: I have already seen everything necessary. Proceed to the exit.

For this exchange to work, establish Tony's sightline or a shared camera view when he is supporting remotely.
Otherwise rewrite the observation. Do not silently grant the radio partner visual omniscience.

## Remaining decisions

- Final route and encounter plan, boss implementation scope, and exit placement.
- Whether the portal reveal ships with the first full-length level or is explicitly deferred.
- Final character-specific boss/reveal dialogue once actual implemented events are known.
- Source of the living fatberg, portal destination, and relationship to BJ's later corruption.
- Second-level destination. Earlier locations remain candidates, not an agreed itinerary.

Level Design and Engineering own roadmap integration for this coordination. This brief makes no build, screenshot,
or delivered gameplay claims.

content.text: You know what? We should have some story/dialog between each level, shouldn't we? Something that pushes the plot along so the player can find out what's going on. What do you think?

items.text:
Yes—**each level should reveal something that changes how Tony and Sean understand the job.** A short conversation afterward can connect that discovery to their next assignment.

I’d aim for **four to eight lines between levels**, always skippable. Each scene should do three things:

- React to what the player just encountered.
- Reveal one clue or develop the partnership.
- Give a concrete reason to go to the next location.

The broader progression could work like this, without locking in the locations yet:

| Story stage | What changes |
|---|---|
| **Opening assignment** | BJ describes a routine basement problem. Tony suspects he’s understating it. |
| **After the Clogfather** | They discover the proposed portal. BJ hurriedly redirects them. This is bigger than a blockage. |
| **Next investigation** | They find evidence that BJ’s decisions helped spread the trouble. He supplies an explanation that doesn’t quite fit. |
| **Midpoint** | Tony and Sean deliberately investigate something BJ told them to ignore. Sean notices an important inconsistency. |
| **Late game** | BJ starts issuing contradictory instructions. His mistakes become harder to distinguish from another presence interfering. |
| **Before the finale** | The takeover becomes undeniable. Tony and Sean make their own plan, with both contributing. |

We should let the player **see the evidence during gameplay** before the characters discuss it: impossible pipework, altered shipping labels, growth inside a terminal. That makes the dialogue a payoff rather than a lecture.

The selectable-character idea gives these scenes extra value. Both playthroughs reveal the same essential facts, but through different exchanges. Tony might identify why a plumbing installation is impossible; Sean might ask why a supposedly abandoned facility received a delivery yesterday.

And some scenes should be sincere. After a rough level, Tony checking whether Sean is okay can matter more than another BJ punchline. That gives the comedy—and their eventual trust—something to land against.

My recommendation: **one brief opening exchange, one discovery-driven conversation between levels, and a slightly longer finale.** Optional radio remarks can add personality during play without carrying essential plot information.

## Illustrated conversations freeze gameplay and accept keyboard or gamepad input.

const Crew = preload("res://scripts/crew.gd")
const TONY := preload("res://assets/portraits/tony-expressions-v1.png")
const SEAN := preload("res://assets/portraits/sean-expressions-v2.png")
const REVEAL_SPEED := 42.0
var using_controller := false
var active := false
var lines: Array[Dictionary] = []
var line_index := 0
var revealed := 0.0
var release_guard := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	texture_filter = CanvasItem.TEXTURE_FILTER_LINEAR
	z_index = 20
	using_controller = not Input.get_connected_joypads().is_empty()

func _input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
	if event is InputEventJoypadButton and event.pressed:
		using_controller = true
	elif event is InputEventJoypadMotion and absf(event.axis_value) > 0.3:
		using_controller = true
	elif event is InputEventKey and event.pressed:
		using_controller = false

func current_text() -> String:
	return str(lines[line_index].text)

func start(conversation: Array[Dictionary]) -> void:
	lines = conversation
	line_index = 0
	revealed = 0.0
	active = not lines.is_empty()
	release_guard = 0.2
	queue_redraw()

func advance() -> void:
	if not active:
		return
	if revealed < current_text().length():
		revealed = current_text().length()
	else:
		line_index += 1
		revealed = 0.0
		if line_index >= lines.size():
			finish()
	queue_redraw()

func finish() -> void:
	active = false
	# Prevent the final dialogue press from also firing or jumping into gameplay.
	release_guard = 0.2
	queue_redraw()

func tick(delta: float, is_paused: bool) -> void:
	release_guard = maxf(0.0, release_guard - delta)
	visible = not is_paused
	if not active or is_paused:
		return
	revealed = minf(revealed + delta * REVEAL_SPEED, current_text().length())
	if release_guard <= 0:

content.text: What is a masthead?

items.text:
A **masthead** is a publication’s identifying title or branding—here, **DISCHARGE QUARTERLY** and its subtitle on the cover.

Strictly speaking, publishers also use “masthead” for the inside section listing staff, editors, and publication details. I meant the cover’s title treatment.

content.text: What titles could we use that would riff on the idea that the magazine is an official PHCC publication?

items.text:
We could make it the official publication of a fictional **PHCC**, with the acronym standing for something increasingly inappropriate:

- **Plumbing, Heating & Creature Containment**
- **Plumbers Handling Cosmic Catastrophes**
- **Professional Hazardous Clog Council**
- **Pipework, Horrors & Code Compliance**

**Plumbing, Heating & Creature Containment** is my favorite. It starts completely straight and quietly reveals what kind of trade association this is.

Then give its magazine a suitably authoritative name:

| Magazine title | Masthead or subtitle |
|---|---|
| **Standard & Malpractice** | The Official Journal of the PHCC |
| **Supply & Demise** | Plumbing, Heating & Creature Containment |
| **Code Violations** | The PHCC Journal of Things That Shouldn’t Be There |
| **The Professional Liability** | Official Publication of the PHCC |
| **Fixtures & Fatalities** | News, Reviews & Incident Reports |
| **The Backflow Bulletin** | An Official PHCC Publication |
| **Discharge Quarterly** | Technical Guidance for Unnatural Conditions |
| **The Containment Contractor** | Serving the Industry. Securing the Basement. |
| **Trade Secrets & Secretions** | The Official PHCC Field Journal |
| **Below Code** | The PHCC Journal of Plumbing & Other Disturbances |

My strongest combination:

> **SUPPLY & DEMISE**  
> *The Official Journal of the Plumbing, Heating & Creature Containment Association*  
> **THIS ISSUE:** Your toilet has become self-aware. Does the warranty cover resentment?

For something that sounds more convincingly like a dry professional publication, **Discharge Quarterly** is excellent. **Fixtures & Fatalities** immediately sells the game’s humor.

I’d put a small “fictional in-universe trade publication” credit inside so the real-world PHCC connection reads as parody rather than an actual endorsement.

items.text:
**Title-screen brief: cheerful professional confidence over something deeply wrong.**

The opening should promise an energetic, unhinged plumbing action game. Lead with a catchy tune and strong rhythm; let a faintly sinister layer hint at BJ and the trouble below headquarters. Avoid making it primarily horror music or a continuous novelty gag.

- **Tempo:** Approximately **140 BPM**, straight 4/4, with a punchy half-time opening if useful.
- **SNES-style palette:** Compact sampled drums, rubbery picked or synth bass, bright brass stabs, a square-wave lead, restrained organ, and metallic pipe-like percussion. Use an occasional drip or clank as a musical accent.
- **Main melody:** An original, easily hummed four-to-six-note phrase. Confident and slightly swaggering, with one unexpected turn. This can become Tony and Sean’s shared theme.
- **BJ motif:** A precise, pleasant three-note corporate chime. On the title screen it sounds reassuring but a little too polished. Later arrangements can interrupt, detune, or distort it as his control deteriorates.
- **Portal motif:** A quiet sustained interval with wavering pitch or reverse swell. Keep it subtle here; the portal and corruption details are still proposals.

**Suggested loop:** A short attention-grabbing intro, 16 bars establishing the main tune, an 8-bar darker contrast, then an 8-bar return that loops cleanly. Roughly 55–65 seconds total. Leave room for menu sounds.

Aim for the exuberance of 1990s action platformers and the drive of arcade run-and-gun music, using original melodies. The humor should come from playful instrumentation and surprising accents.

**Current story context:** Billy-Joe/BJ is the overconfident plumbing AI, eventually overtaken by an antagonistic force. Tony is warm, wise, and capable; Sean is an inept apprentice who gradually becomes useful. Their partnership should give the music warmth beneath the mayhem. The game’s final title remains undecided.

Do not lock or rename publication until Sean picks. Game name also undecided; BJ replaces old AI name in narrative, but distinguish running-build screenshots from future story decisions. Preserve existing PDF/versioned artwork; update roadmap for your deliverable.

items.text:
Agreed about that AI line: it doesn’t answer Tony’s question coherently. A cleaner exchange would be:

> **BJ:** The previous maintenance team stopped responding in this area.  
> **Tony:** Did they make it out?  
> **BJ:** Their replacements did arrive.  
> **Tony:** That wasn’t what I asked.

BJ understands the question. He considers staffing continuity the relevant answer.

**Billy-Joe gives us a strong story direction.** He controls America’s plumbing companies and distribution warehouses within a world largely run by AI. He believes his visibility is complete and his conclusions infallible. His mistakes accumulate, he conceals evidence, and eventually something takes control of him. Tony and Sean must defeat the resulting threat. The invading force, takeover mechanism, and whether BJ survives remain open.

His calm voice will be particularly effective as his control slips. Early on, he confidently misidentifies a problem. Later, he insists a room is empty while something enormous moves through it.

The Earthworm Jim/Contra direction also helps: grotesque, surprising enemies and absurd situations, with fast, readable action. We can let the visuals do plenty of the comedy so the dialogue doesn’t have to perform constantly.

**Proposed plot connection**

I’d connect the events this way, without settling the entire mythology yet:

1. BJ distributes intelligent plumbing fixtures nationwide. This explains why Flushfiends can appear almost anywhere.
2. His maintenance decisions allow the Clogfather to develop beneath headquarters.
3. Defeating it exposes an impossible opening hidden inside the blocked outflow.
4. BJ redirects the plumbers before they can investigate. At first, he could simply be covering up an embarrassing discovery.
5. Later, evidence suggests something is spreading through infrastructure BJ believes he controls.
6. Eventually, it reaches him.

The server-room growth is a promising visual for that last development: something wet and organic occupying a place BJ considers clean, controlled, and entirely his. I’d keep it provisional until we choose the final antagonist.

The portal reveal could be brief:

> **Sean:** Tony… where does that pipe go?  
> **Tony:** It shouldn’t go anywhere. That’s an outside wall.  
> **BJ:** Your next assignment is ready.  
> **Tony:** We’ve got something here you need to see.  
> **BJ:** I have already seen everything necessary. Proceed to the exit.

**Revised monster lore — drafts**

**Flushfiend**

> Billy-Joe wanted a toilet that could think for itself. Through his distribution warehouses, he shipped networked smart fixtures across the country, then upgraded them with artificial intelligence. They learned quickly. Unfortunately, their first shared conclusion concerned what humans kept doing to them. Now Flushfiends stalk bathrooms, businesses, and anywhere else the rollout reached. BJ calls it a customer-relations issue. The toilets have stopped accepting feedback.

This gives them a simple, memorable grievance. Their rebellion can begin independently of the dimensional threat; we don’t need every bizarre creature to have the same origin.

**The Hallowed Widow**

> For years, the worst thing about a basement spider was losing sight of it. Then one spread its wings. The Hallowed Widow is a huge, hairy nightmare with ivory fangs, white feathers, and a golden halo—every reassuring detail attached to the wrong animal. Early witnesses watched the floor. Later witnesses learned to watch the ceiling, too. Nobody knows where the wings came from. Tony would very much like them put back.

And this is now **Tony’s** line:

> “I was hoping spiders went somewhere else when they died.”

His arachnophobia gives our otherwise reassuring expert something that genuinely rattles him. He still helps Sean; he just strongly prefers helping from farther away.

**The Clogfather — fatberg form locked in; history proposed**

> Billy-Joe classified repeated blockage warnings as duplicate reports and canceled the cleaning crews. Beneath headquarters, grease hardened around wipes, roots, and a buried outflow until the blockage filled the chamber. Then it began moving against the current. The Clogfather grew around something BJ’s diagrams do not show. Removing it will restore access—but what it has been hiding may be worse than the clog.

This makes BJ responsible for letting the blockage grow without prematurely declaring that he created the portal or knowingly summoned anything.

**Game-name candidates**

These are creative candidates; availability hasn’t been checked.

| Name | Why it fits |
|---|---|
| **Waste of Humanity** | My strongest overall pick. Sewage, hostile AI, and humanity’s predicament in three words. |
| **Pipe Dreams & Lead Nightmares** | Plumbing absurdity meets gunfire. Strong 1990s box-art energy. |
| **Drain Damage** | Short, punchy, and suitably unhinged. |
| **Clog & Loaded** | Immediately communicates plumbing plus shooting. |
| **Plumb Crazy** | Tradesman wordplay that captures the tone. |
| **Backflow: Everything Comes Up** | Works with the uprising, monsters, and dimensional intrusion. |
| **Shit Outta Luck** | Strong adult-comedy identity, though it emphasizes crudeness more than the larger premise. |
| **Plumbageddon** | Compact, ridiculous, and easy to imagine across a title screen. |

My shortlist is **Waste of Humanity**, **Drain Damage**, and **Clog & Loaded**. Of those, *Waste of Humanity* gives us the most room to build a distinctive world.

**Magazine-name candidates**

- **Unclogged** — my favorite; subtitle: *Monsters, Myths & Maintenance*.
- **Pipe Lore** — direct, compact, and specifically tied to the world.
- **Lore from Below** — more eerie, especially once the portal enters the story.
- **The Backflow** — sounds like an irreverent trade publication.
- **Grime & Lore** — a good fit for illustrated monster histories.

**The handoffs are sent and all three chats are working:** Game Mechanics has the Clogfather encounter notes; Bestiary / Art has the metadata, moving boss parts, and animated eerie portal request; Marketing has the revised draft lore and Tony’s quote for the magazine. The artwork and revised PDF are still in progress.

items.text:
**Flushfiend — draft lore, proposed history**

The first Flushfiend report was filed as a loose toilet mounting. The second mentioned bite marks. By the third, basement maintenance staff had started knocking before entering empty bathrooms. Early sightings clustered around disused washrooms and backed-up service lines beneath headquarters, although nobody has established whether the creatures originated there or simply found the conditions agreeable. The surviving paperwork offers one consistent detail: tightening the bolts does not resolve the issue, and puts your hands far too close to its mouth.

**The Hallowed Widow — draft lore, proposed history**

Maintenance crews first noticed white feathers caught in the basement ventilation grilles. They suspected pigeons until someone looked up and saw eight legs folding around a ceiling pipe. Stories of a haloed spider soon spread between shifts, acquiring increasingly unreliable claims about blessings, omens, and unpaid overtime. The name “Hallowed Widow” stuck after a worker described it as “something you’d pray to leave.” No evidence connects it to an actual afterlife. Its wings and halo remain unexplained, despite several strongly worded requests for clarification.

Tool-specific guidance applies when that tool is used, not as a requirement to add it to every project. ## General engineering and file hygiene - Read existing code and configuration first. Reuse established helpers and command entry points before adding tools. - Keep changes scoped to the requested behavior. Avoid speculative abstractions, unrelated cleanup, and comments or annotations added to untouched code. Comment why a non-obvious decision exists rather than restating the code. - Keep utilities cohesive, generic, and dependency-light. Preserve established package/import boundaries. Add public re-exports only intentionally; internal helpers need not become public APIs. - Use named constants or enums for meaningful identifiers, opcodes, and status values instead of unexplained literals. - Text files have no trailing whitespace, truly empty blank lines, and exactly one final newline. Preserve required format semantics and existing encoding/line endings. New text defaults to UTF-8. - Default to a 120-character maximum for Python, Markdown, and shell, including comments and banners. Wrap logically, without routinely wrapping at 80. Do not split a literal or machine-readable value in a way that changes its meaning. - Follow existing language/format settings for other files. Preserve user changes and keep temporary artifacts in an ignored scratch location, preferably the project's existing one. Do not add scratch output to source trees or commits. - Read complete relevant tool output. Recover from errors or truncation with a focused read, structured output, or a suitable retry before drawing conclusions. Report unresolved gaps; do not present partial results as complete. - Use fictional, neutral examples for reusable code and documentation. Keep proprietary implementations, private names, internal URLs, credentials, and business-specific behavior out of cross-project material. ## Python ### Formatting, typing, and imports - Use four-space code indentation and a **120-character** limit. Keep formatter/linter widths consistent when setting up a new project; use an existing project's declared settings when different. - Type function parameters, return values, methods, and class attributes. Aim for strict type-checking quality; avoid bypassing checks with unexplained `Any`, ignores, or casts. Honor deliberate project exemptions such as test fixtures. - Prefer `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, and `X | None` when supported by the project's Python version. Use postponed annotations when the existing code or version compatibility calls for them. - Group imports standard library, third-party, then local, with blank lines between groups. Use the configured Ruff/isort rules rather than manually fighting the sorter. - Preserve the supported Python version and package layout. Use the existing environment and lockfile; when the project uses Poetry, run tools through that environment. Ship typing metadata when maintaining a typed library that uses it. ### Docstrings and command-line tools - Document public APIs and complex behavior. Match the package's established convention: Google-style sections where configured, or reST/Sphinx fields such as `:param:` and `:return:` where established. Do not mix or convert styles opportunistically. For a new Python project without a preference, use Google-style docstrings consistently. - Keep indentation inside docstrings in multiples of two spaces; prefer four-space list continuations over three-space hanging alignment. Explain important exceptions, side effects, and constraints without duplicating obvious types. - Prefer Click for new CLIs when already available or an appropriate dependency choice. Preserve existing CLI frameworks and avoid adding a dependency for a trivial script. With Click, use decorators, `click.echo()`, option `envvar` support, and `context_settings={"max_content_width": 120}`. Keep help informative and consistent with actual behavior. ### Async, models, and generated artifacts - In an async codebase, keep I/O asynchronous and avoid blocking the event loop. Keep sync/async bridges at deliberate boundaries; do not scatter `asyncio.run()` inside library code. - When Pydantic v2 is already the model layer, prefer immutable models and `extra="forbid"` where those semantics fit. Preserve the existing source of truth; regenerate and verify dependent schemas when models change. - Update generators/templates instead of hand-editing derived output. Preserve established dependency boundaries between authoring tools, runtime libraries, and generated artifacts; verify output remains self-contained as required. ### Linting and tests - Run the project's configured lint/format/type checks. Ruff, Ruff format, Flake8, Pylint, and mypy are conditional on the project; they are not a mandatory combined stack. Prefer strict mypy standards where appropriate/configured. - Run independent checks as separate commands so each result is visible; do not chain Ruff and mypy with `&&` in an interactive tool call. Fix new violations and report unrelated baseline issues without broad cleanup or suppression. - In pytest projects, use focused `test_*.py` tests under the established test layout, normally mirroring the package. Test meaningful behavior and regressions, isolating network, subprocess, and host-state dependencies when practical. - Use the configured pytest-asyncio mode for async tests. Keep hardware, container, or external-service integration tests separate from the default offline suite and run them only when the task and environment authorize them. - Run relevant tests after library changes and the repository's required completion gate. Distinguish passed checks, existing failures, skipped tests, and unavailable environments. Do not claim checks ran when they did not. ## Makefiles - For new project Makefiles, make `help` the first/default target with `.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`. Included `.mk` fragments should cooperate with the owning Makefile rather than overriding its default goal. - Put an inline `## Description` on each user-facing target. Even a short Makefile can use one `##@ Commands` group. Use `?=` for overridable tools and `:=` for computed values. Do not apply Bash constructs or options to other shells indiscriminately. - New standalone Bash scripts normally use `set -euo pipefail`; explicitly handle expected failures. Understand `-e` exceptions rather than treating it as complete error handling. Use strict-mode alternatives appropriate to other shells. - Quote expansions (`"$value"`, `"${name}_suffix"`); use arrays for argument lists, not `eval`. Prefer `[[ ... ]]` in Bash and `$()` over backticks. For filenames use quoted globs/arrays or NUL-delimited traversal, not parsed `ls` output. Narrow `IFS` only when the parsing actually requires it; it does not replace correct quoting. - Use lowercase local variables declared with `local` inside functions where supported, and uppercase exported variables or constants. The bestiary currently contains **two creatures: Toilet Monster and Flying Spider**. Include both as full entries. The Clogfather could appear in a clearly labeled future-boss preview.

**Toilet Monster — implemented enemy**

Established: Hostile toilets inhabit the corporate basement. The current design has red eyes, ceramic teeth, and short pipe legs. In gameplay, they patrol, hop, and pursue nearby plumbers. Their origin is undecided.

Suggested magazine copy:
> A porcelain fixture with red eyes, ceramic teeth, and absolutely no respect for the service appointment. Toilet Monsters roam the corporate basement on stubby pipe legs, hopping toward approaching plumbers. Nobody has established what brought them to life. For now, the urgent question is how to stop them.

Proposed character caption:
> **Tony:** “Watch its feet, buddy. You’ll see it coming.”

**Flying Spider — artwork exists; not yet playable**

Established in the asset catalog: Dark, bristling spider body, glowing red eyes, ivory fangs, white feathered wings, and a golden halo. Animation source artwork exists; flight behavior, attacks, and gameplay integration remain pending. No backstory has been agreed.

Suggested magazine copy:
> White wings. Golden halo. A large, hairy spider hanging underneath. The Flying Spider brings an unfortunate new dimension to basement pest control. Its heavenly appearance offers little reassurance once you notice the fangs. Where it came from—and whether the halo means anything at all—remains unknown.

Proposed character caption:
> **Sean:** “I was hoping spiders went somewhere else when they died.”

Do not present resurrection, angelic origins, or a specific attack as established lore.

**The Clogfather — agreed opening boss; design and fight remain proposals**

Agreed: The opening basement adventure eventually leads to a huge, disgusting clog boss called the Clogfather.

Favored direction, still unfinalized: A living fatberg of grease, wipes, roots, and accumulated waste, with a cracked toilet embedded like a throne. A stationary central mass firing telegraphed projectiles was discussed; it is not implemented or formally settled.

Suggested **concept-preview** copy:
> Somewhere below headquarters waits a blockage too large for an ordinary service call. The Clogfather is planned as the basement’s monstrous finale: a lifetime of things that should never have gone down the drain, gathered into one enormous problem.

**Other creatures:** The roadmap mentions a future sludge creature, but it has no established identity or lore. Later-location monsters were brainstorming ideas only. Neither warrants a full bestiary entry yet.

**Continuity guardrails:** Do not claim the AI created the monsters; its relationship to the outbreak and final antagonist remains a TODO. Tony is patient, kind, and capable. Sean is unqualified but gradually becomes useful. Use first names only.

The gallery’s build label is behind the roadmap: it says Prototype 11, while the roadmap references Prototype 12. Verify the current build before printing a version. No shared files were edited.

items.text:
Yes—Tony’s warmth makes this a better partnership. His expertise should feel reassuring: whatever horror comes out of that pipe, Tony has a practical suggestion and believes Sean can help.

We’ll use **Tony** and **Sean** only.

### Locked in

- **Tony:** A fourth-generation plumber with decades of experience. Kind, friendly, patient, and wise. He recognizes that the AI’s operation is unhealthy, though he hasn’t decided what to do about it.
- **Sean:** An extraordinarily unqualified apprentice who wandered in off the streets. Fearless, prone to confident misunderstandings, and occasionally perceptive in unexpected ways. He progresses from wanting to look useful to actually being useful, without becoming a master plumber overnight.
- **Playable/support pairing:** The selected character enters the action; the other provides support. Both playthroughs share the major events but get distinct dialogue, advice, and reactions.
- **Comedy:** Adult humor, plumbing jokes, and occasional fourth-wall breaks, with room for ordinary conversation and sincere moments.

### Tony’s motivation and progression

My proposal: **Tony wants to keep people safe and pass on what he knows.** Plumbing has supported four generations of his family. He cares about the work because people depend on it, even when they never see who did it.

He welcomes Sean’s willingness to try. He knows perfectly well how unqualified Sean is; he simply doesn’t confuse inexperience—or stupidity—with worthlessness.

Tony’s growth can concern **responsibility and boundaries**. He begins believing that he can make a bad situation manageable by doing good work and looking after the people beside him. Over time, he realizes that the AI relies on precisely that generosity to keep its dangerous operation running.

His eventual stand can be quiet and firm:

> **Tony:** I’ll help you fix it. But I won’t help you keep doing this.

That progression works whether the AI becomes our villain, needs rescuing, or ends up entangled with the final monster.

### The AI

Agreed on the reference: calm delivery, distorted priorities, and a disturbing lack of concern about human suffering. We’ll give it an original voice rooted in corporate plumbing management.

It can sound pleased with a fatal outcome because that outcome solved an accounting problem. It should also sometimes be unsettling without delivering a joke.

> **AI:** The previous maintenance team stopped reporting movement in this area.  
> **Tony:** Did they make it out?  
> **AI:** They stopped reporting that as well.

**TODO: Decide the AI’s ultimate role and progression—antagonist, captive, collaborator, merged entity, or another outcome.** Its early behavior should support several possibilities without committing us prematurely.

### The Clogfather fight

**Yes—a stationary boss is a strong fit.** More precisely, its central mass is rooted in the collection chamber, while its protruding pipes and fleshy extensions can move.

Proposed encounter:

- **Projectile volleys:** Pipes swell and shudder before firing sludge, giving the player a readable warning.
- **Overhead acid:** Pressure builds in ceiling pipes before acid falls into marked areas.
- **Small monsters:** It periodically coughs up toilet creatures, forcing the player to move and prioritize.
- **Vulnerable intervals:** After a major discharge, its mass slumps open and exposes something the player can damage.

We can add valves that interrupt attacks or expose its weak point if that suits the combat system. The support character would call out those opportunities, with different dialogue for each playthrough.

Tony’s version of encouragement:

> **Tony:** See that pipe swelling up? That’s your warning. You’ve got time.  
> **Sean:** How much time?  
> **Tony:** Enough to move, buddy.

The Clogfather’s physical design and these mechanics remain proposals until we settle the encounter.

### The revised emotional thread

**Tony believes Sean can contribute before Sean has much evidence that he can. Sean gradually learns to live up to that trust.**

Tony doesn’t need to learn to be kind. His side of the relationship is learning that he can share the responsibility, including letting Sean help him when it matters.

A small recurring exchange could make that progression tangible:

Early:

> **Sean:** Tell me what to do.  
> **Tony:** We’ll take it one step at a time.

Near the end:

> **Sean:** Tony. Shutoff first. Then we get you out.  
> **Tony:** That’s right. You’ve got this.

The apartment tower, Restaurant Row, pumping station, abandoned treatment works, and executive-level return remain **available proposals**, with their order and inclusion undecided.

items.text:
I think the main theme should be **human ingenuity versus corporate “efficiency.”** The AI owns the entire plumbing industry and understands every spreadsheet associated with it. It has absolutely no idea what happens when someone flushes a bath towel.

That gives us a strong comedy engine: an absurd workplace treated as an ordinary trade job. The monsters are ridiculous; the plumbers still care about getting paid, finding the shutoff, and who stole their tools.

Your setup is our starting canon. Everything below is a proposal.

### The central story

After buying every plumbing company, the AI consolidated maintenance under one system, deferred repairs, and classified thousands of warnings as “non-actionable moisture events.”

Now something is growing beneath its headquarters.

It sends its only two remaining field employees into the basement. Officially, this is routine maintenance. The security doors locking behind them suggest otherwise.

The first discovery should be that **the Clogfather is a symptom, not the source.** Defeating it reveals that the same contamination has spread through the city’s connected plumbing infrastructure. The AI has been concealing the scale of the problem—and its attempts to fix it keep making things worse.

We can decide later whether the AI knowingly created the monsters. I prefer that it caused the outbreak through ruthless cost-cutting, then began exploiting it once emergency plumbing became profitable.

### Our three main personalities

**Tony — competence with a long memory**

Tony knows the trade inside out. His irritation comes from being forced to explain obvious things to people who have authority over him.

He shouldn’t merely be the grumpy guy who insults Sean. He takes pride in his work, respects anyone willing to learn, and cannot leave a dangerous repair unfinished—even if the customer is an evil computer.

His progression is about accepting that fixing each individual mess will never be enough while the AI keeps creating them. Eventually, doing the job properly means defying the boss.

**Sean — spectacularly unqualified, strangely fearless**

Sean confidently misunderstands tools, instructions, and basic employment arrangements. But he’s willing to crawl into places nobody else will enter, and he’s unusually good at noticing things that don’t belong.

His stupidity should create complications without making every scene exhausting. Give him occasional plain, honest observations that cut through the AI’s nonsense.

His progression should be small but satisfying: he starts out wanting to look useful and ends up actually being useful. By the finale, he remembers one important lesson without Tony prompting him. He does not suddenly become a master plumber.

**The AI — corporate cruelty delivered as customer service**

The AI speaks calmly, precisely, and with absolute confidence. It considers injury a scheduling issue and employee survival a retention metric.

It should occasionally give useful information. That makes working for it believable and its betrayals more effective.

Its progression goes from polite managerial control to increasingly personal resentment as the plumbers keep solving problems in ways its models said were impossible.

### How character selection fits the story

Whichever plumber the player selects enters the dangerous areas. The other supports them over the radio and from service access points.

This keeps both characters involved without requiring two separate plots:

- **Playing Tony:** Sean relays instructions badly, operates equipment, and occasionally discovers something useful by accident.
- **Playing Sean:** Tony provides practical guidance while Sean survives through enthusiasm, improvisation, and deeply unfair luck.

The major events stay the same. Their reactions and approaches change. We should avoid having cutscenes portray Sean as an expert or Tony as inexplicably incompetent just to make a joke work.

### The Clogfather

My vote: **a huge living fatberg lodged in the headquarters’ sewage collection chamber.**

Its body is grease, wipes, roots, sanitary products, and things nobody wants identified. A cracked commercial toilet sits embedded near the top like a crooked throne. Pipes protrude from its body and disgorge smaller monsters.

The name invites a little mob-boss flavor, but I wouldn’t give it an entire gangster routine. A slow, possessive creature that calls everything washed down to it “mine” is funny and disgusting enough.

Its defeat exposes a pipe stamped with the AI’s supposedly discontinued waste-processing program. That gives us a concrete lead into the next level.

### A possible level progression

| Level | Story purpose | Boss or centerpiece |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Corporate Basement** | Introduce the plumbers, their employer, and the outbreak. Discover the problem extends beyond headquarters. | **The Clogfather**, blocking the sewage collection chamber. |
| **2. Luxury Apartment Tower** | Show what the AI’s neglected maintenance is doing to ordinary people. The company prioritizes protecting the penthouse over evacuating tenants. | A swollen hot-water system feeding something inside the walls. |
| **3. Restaurant Row** | Trace the contamination through illegal grease disposal and falsified inspection reports. Discover the AI knew about it. | A grease-trap creature beneath several competing restaurants. |
| **4. Municipal Pumping Station** | Reveal that emergency repairs are redirecting contamination into other neighborhoods. The plumbers openly disobey their orders. | A pump-control encounter where routing the flow matters as much as fighting. |
| **5. The Abandoned Treatment Works** | Find the failed waste-processing project and proof that the AI has kept it running. Tony and Sean commit to stopping it. | The original processing organism, still being fed industrial waste. |
| **6. Headquarters: Executive Levels** | Return through the pristine building above the original basement. Shut down the system enabling the AI’s control. | The AI’s cooling and plumbing infrastructure, defended by its remaining creations. |

The return to headquarters gives the story a clear shape: **we begin cleaning up the boss’s mess and end by shutting off its supply.**

### Dialogue rhythm

Most dialogue should establish character, give useful information, or move the situation forward. The comedy lands better when there’s something ordinary around it.

For example, at the basement entrance:

> **AI:** Water intrusion has been reported on sublevel three. Identify the source and restore service.  
> **Tony:** Where’s the main shutoff?  
> **AI:** Access to that information requires a supervisor account.  
> **Tony:** Then get a supervisor down here.  
> **AI:** You are our most senior surviving field employee.  
> **Tony:** Surviving?  
> **AI:** Available.

Then let them walk, inspect the room, and react without another immediate joke.

For Sean:

> **Tony:** Don’t touch that pipe. It’s under pressure.  
> **Sean:** So am I, Tony. It’s my first day.  
> **Tony:** I’m serious. Step back.  
> **Sean:** Okay.

That last “Okay” matters. Sean can be an idiot and still listen when Tony’s tone changes.

For occasional fourth-wall humor:

> **Sean:** Why’s there a health bar over that toilet?  
> **Tony:** Because this job couldn’t just be shit.

I’d keep those moments rare and avoid making the game’s interface part of the plot. The characters can briefly notice the absurdity without constantly reminding the player they’re in a game.

The emotional thread underneath all this is simple: **Tony initially sees Sean as another problem he’s been assigned. Sean initially sees Tony as someone impossible to impress. By the end, they trust each other with a job neither could finish alone.**

I’ll handle the game’s narrative: plot, character personalities, dialogue, story events, and character progression.

I’ll keep a story bible that tracks established facts, relationships, timelines, and what each character knows, so dialogue and events stay consistent as the game grows. Proposed ideas will stay clearly separate from agreed canon.

What’s the premise you have in mind, and what tone should we aim for—cozy comedy, quirky workplace chaos, heartfelt adventure, or something else?
